title: Sabbath economics
hookLine: rest, gleaning and jubilee limit greed

cards: Harvest time in ancient Israel. A farmer walks the edge of his barley field with a sickle, and right where he could take the last good rows, he stops. The corners stay standing.
The stalks his workers dropped stay on the ground. Later, a widow and a stranger from out of town walk in behind them and gather what was left, and nobody chases them off.
The farmer isn't being sloppy, and he isn't being nice. He's obeying the law. The Bible builds limits right into the economy.

teach.b: It starts with a day. The commandment in Exodus gives six days for work and the seventh for rest, and it spells out who rests: not only the family, but the servants, the animals and the stranger too.
Deuteronomy repeats the commandment and adds a reason: the rest is given "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou."
And then: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt." A people who remember being servants are told to let their own servants rest. Rest isn't a reward for the people at the top.

Then the harvest law in Leviticus: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." Those are left, the text says, for the poor and the stranger.
And then the boldest one, jubilee.

Leviticus describes a fiftieth year when land returns to the families who first held it, and the trumpet tells the people to "proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof."

Leviticus doesn't say whether the jubilee was ever fully kept. But the idea is plain: nobody's gain is meant to swallow a neighbor forever, because, as God says in the same chapter, "the land is mine."

The manna story from earlier in this stretch belongs to the same family: bread that spoiled when it was hoarded. Christians who speak of Sabbath economics read all of these together: rest, gleaning, release.
Each one puts a fence around greed. Each one says there is enough, if nobody takes it all.

how: Some Christians and churches take up Sabbath economics through practices like a weekly day without shopping, food gleaning projects that gather leftover crops for the poor, and jubilee campaigns for debt relief.

games.q: you're the farmer. the barley is good, prices are high, and the corners of your field are full of grain. what does the law tell you to do?
o: harvest every row; it's your land.
leave the corners and the dropped stalks for the poor and the stranger.
harvest it all, then give some away later if you feel like it.
games.why: Leviticus says leave the corners and the gleanings standing. it isn't charity after the fact; the limit is built into the harvest itself.

practice: Picture a day with no purchases at all, no tapping a card, no cart, no quick snack on the way home, and notice which purchase is hardest to imagine skipping.
Then picture what you already have: food in the cupboard, clothes on the hook, a roof. If you pray, you can give thanks for what's already in the house.

wordCard.voice: Sabbath economics. The Bible's limits on greed, read together: rest for everyone, servants included, corners left for the poor, and a jubilee of release.

carryVoice: Your line: enough for all. The corners of the field were left for others. Until next time.
